newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu, PLO's Arafat meet over Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu, PLO's Arafat meet over Hebron.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Tuesday in a U.S.-mediated bid to seal a deal by Christmas on a long-stymied Israeli handover of the West Bank town of Hebron.

Before the meeting opened, U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, who has shepherded the talks since arriving in the area on Saturday, dampened expectations that a deal on an Israeli redeployment in Hebron could be sealed on Tuesday.
"We have clearly energised negotiations over the last couple of days," Ross told reporters, but added: "I don't expect that one meeting is going to conclude this."

Netanyahu and Arafat last met at an emergency summit in Washington called by U.S. President Bill Clinton after clashes between Israeli and Palestinian security forces that killed 75 people in September.

Israeli media had speculated that the sides could wrap up an accord by Christmas Day as a "holiday present" to Clinton, who has nudged forward the difficult talks between the two sides since they signed a landmark deal in 1993.
Israel and the PLO have accused each other of foot-dragging in nearly three months of talks on Hebron, most of which was due to have been handed over to Palestinian self-rule last March.

Netanyahu has said he would sign an agreement only if it guaranteed the safety of the 400 Jewish settlers who live among more than 100,000 Arabs in the West Bank town, a longtime hotbed of Moslem and Jewish militancy.

The pullout is seen as key to any further Israeli-PLO peace moves. Arabs view the pullout, promised by Israel's former Labour government, as an acid test of Netanyahu's intentions toward the Middle East peace process as a whole.
The talks, which seemed near ruin in recent weeks, came to life over the weekend with the arrival of Ross, who shuttled between Israel, Gaza and Egypt to try to broker a deal.
Ross's last mission collapsed in October.

Netanyahu spokesman Shai Bazak, speaking after the two leaders had met for some 90 minutes, also voiced reservations the deal could be clinched on Tuesday: "From our standpoint, this is apparently a working meeting, and it's possible more meetings will be needed to close the matter."
After coming to power in June, Netanyahu had resisted meeting Arafat, once vilified by the Israeli leader's Likud party as a "master terrorist".

The surprise progress towards a Hebron accord sent shock waves through Hebron's Jewish population. "We're crossing our fingers that this agreement, which, heaven forbid, will bring catastrophe on the Jewish community ... will not be signed," Hebron resident Moshe Ben-Zimra told Israel Radio.

Palestinian officials have said Israel has dropped its insistence on having the right of "hot pursuit" of Palestinian suspects into PLO-held areas, accepting instead existing language in the Hebron handover agreement signed in 1995.

A PLO official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters: "They still have problems over two main issues. The location of joint mobile units and the distance between Israeli and Palestinian checkpoints."
Under peace deals that have led to army pullouts from much of the Gaza Strip and from seven West Bank towns, Israeli and Palestinian forces conduct joint security patrols.
The issues of joint patrols and the distance separating the sides became a focus of discussion after 15 Israeli soldiers and 60 Palestinians were killed in gun battles in September.
That bloodshed erupted after Netanyahu approved opening a tunnel near Islamic holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem.
Another PLO official said that if remaining issues were resolved, a deal could be announced by the two leaders and the troop pullback from 80 percent of the city would begin within hours.
Israel's Maariv daily said that the army, given the green light, could execute the pullout within half an hour.
